summary: Commander Sol 7 is a free, interactive 3D browser game where kids aged 7–12 run a Mars outpost for seven sols. You stand inside the habitat in first person: drag to look around 360°, watch the Sun through the glass, and press real controls on the console (solar-panel lever, airlock, radio, water valve, storm alarm). Every sol brings an event, and every choice costs something: Power, Life support, Crew health or Science. Short cutscenes show what you chose, like a first-person spacewalk or the panels folding, and blinking warning lights tell you when a bar runs low. The missions come from real NASA space weather. Play a historical Sun (September 2017, May 2024, October 2024) or today's Sun, which uses live data from NASA DONKI. The page always shows whether the data is live or a saved copy. The game is in English and Spanish, and your missions are saved in a mission log you can move to another device with a link or QR code. No accounts, no ads, no real names, and no data leaves the player's browser. Kids learn that space weather is real and that engineering is about trade-offs, not one right answer.
details:
WHAT IT IS

Commander Sol 7 is a free, no-install browser game for kids aged 7–12, built for the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. The player commands a small Mars outpost and must survive seven sols (Martian days). Every sol brings one event, and every decision trades one resource for another.

THE PROBLEM

Kids rarely get to feel what mission control feels: you cannot protect everything at once. Space weather (solar flares, coronal mass ejections, particle storms) is invisible, real, and one of the biggest risks for astronauts, but it is almost never taught in a way kids can play with.

HOW IT PLAYS

- Interactive 3D: you are inside the habitat in first person. Drag (or use the arrow keys) to look 360°. The Sun shines through the glass, and a monitor shows the sol, the event and your bars.

- Decisions are physical controls in the cabin: a lever to fold the solar panels, an airlock, a water valve, a radio to Earth, a tool kit, a storm alarm, lamps, a pantry, a battery and a science station. Each one glows and has a label. Text buttons are always available as an alternative.

- Cutscenes: after each choice, a short scene shows what happened (a first-person spacewalk in a helmet, the panels folding, the shelter alarm, the water flowing). Players can skip them.

- Warnings: when Power, Life support or Crew health get low, a red strip, a blinking light, a red cabin lamp and an alarm tell the player what to fix.

- Two views: switch between the cabin and an outside view of the base.

- Resources: Power, Life support and Crew health, plus Science points. Cosmic radiation lowers crew health every sol, so even a quiet day costs something.

- Six events: quiet sol, greenhouse, dust storm, communications failure, solar flare and coronal mass ejection. Flares and dust storms have a 10-second countdown that can be turned off in Settings.

- Score = Science + sols survived + how healthy the bars are. Playing it safe keeps you alive but earns little. Taking risks can earn more, or end the mission.

- Sound and music: sound effects and a calm background track, both on/off in Settings.

REAL NASA DATA, LIVE AND SAVED

- Source: NASA DONKI (Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information), from the Community Coordinated Modeling Center at NASA Goddard: solar flares, coronal mass ejections, solar energetic particle events and geomagnetic storms.

- Historical Suns use real DONKI events saved in the game: September 2017 (including the X9.3 and X8.2 flares and a 2,650 km/s CME), May 2024 and October 2024.

- "Today's Sun" uses live data: the game asks DONKI for the last 30 days and builds your missions from what the Sun actually did. A green badge reads "LIVE · NASA DONKI" with the time.

- If NASA cannot be reached, a yellow badge says so, gives the reason, and the game uses the last saved copy. Nothing is ever shown as live when it is not.

- Real facts in the game: Mars is 1.524 AU from the Sun, so a flare's light takes about 13 minutes to arrive; a CME's arrival time is distance divided by its measured speed; radio between Earth and Mars takes 3 to 22 minutes one way; in September 2017 a solar storm more than doubled the radiation measured by NASA's Curiosity rover on Mars. Real event IDs and classes are shown to the player.

SAVED GAMES AND PROGRESS

Every finished mission goes into a mission log with charts of Power, Life support and Crew health. Progress can be moved to another browser or device with a link or a QR code. Nothing is uploaded or downloaded: the log travels inside the link.

LANGUAGES, ACCESSIBILITY AND PRIVACY

- English and Spanish (English by default, Spanish in Settings).

- Large and extra-large text, a reduce-motion option, and sound/music switches.

- No accounts, no ads and no tracking. The commander gets a made-up nickname, never a real name. Progress stays in the player's own browser unless they choose to share the link.

WHAT KIDS LEARN

- Space weather is real, and you can read it in NASA data.

- Engineers decide with trade-offs: protecting the crew costs power or science.

- Delay matters: Mars is far from Earth, so the crew often has to decide on its own.

SOUND, ART AND TECH

All sound effects and music are generated by code in the browser, and the pixel-art sun logo is drawn in code (SVG). No audio or image files are used, and no AI-generated images, video or audio appear in the game. Built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Three.js for the 3D scene, a Netlify function to reach NASA DONKI, and hosted on Netlify.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE

The game concept, rules, balance and data selection are by my team (7rauma7ic). AI assistants (Claude by Anthropic) helped with brainstorming, research, filtering the NASA data, writing and translation, and writing and debugging code. The team reviewed and tested everything. This disclosure is also inside the game ("About the data") and in the project files.
